title: Modify System Image
summary: Modify System Image describes adversary changes to the operating system of an embedded network device, such as a router, switch or firewall, in order to weaken defences and add capabilities. These devices normally use a monolithic design: the operating system and nearly all device functionality live inside a single image file, which the boot process loads and runs. That concentration is what makes the technique powerful and what shapes its artefacts. Instead of installing separate programs, the adversary either replaces or patches that one image, and every function the device performs afterwards can be affected. The change can be applied to non volatile storage, so the tampered image loads on the next boot, or it can be made in the running memory of a live device for immediate effect without touching the stored copy. Storage changes survive a reset and are therefore persistent, while memory only changes are lost at reboot unless something in the boot chain also maintains them. Once the image is modified, the device can be made to weaken encryption, authentication or boundary filtering, to provide new services such as hidden proxies or keystroke capture, or to report false information, including version strings that hide a downgrade. Detection relies on integrity verification of image files against vendor hashes, comparison of stored and running versions, review of image transfer logs and boot variable changes, and behavioural baselines that expose new listening ports, new outbound connections or unexpected configuration content. Legitimate image management happens through documented procedures with matching hashes and change records.

beginner.definition: On many network devices, the entire operating system is stored in one single file, called the system image. This technique describes an attacker changing that file. The change can be saved for the next start, or made in memory while the device runs.
beginner.whyItMatters: One file controls almost everything the device does, including its security checks. Changing it lets an attacker weaken protection, add hidden features or make the device report false information. Because the device keeps working normally, users and staff notice nothing. You need integrity checks and honest baselines to catch it.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains a high level of access to the network device.
They load a modified operating system image onto the device storage area.
They set the device to boot from that altered image the next time.
Alternatively, they patch the running system directly in memory, leaving no stored change.
The device then carries out its normal tasks using the changed instructions.
Hidden features may work and security checks may quietly stop doing their job.
beginner.example: Think of a factory machine that runs from a single control board. Change that board and you change everything the machine does, from how fast it runs to which safety guards activate. A saboteur cannot rewire the whole factory, but he can swap that one board for a copy he has altered. The machine still starts, still produces, and the gauges still show normal readings. Only the instructions have changed. Modifying a system image works the same way, and if he reprogrammes the board while it runs, the change disappears once the machine restarts.
takeaways: Verify system image hashes, because a modified image still runs normally.
Record which image each device boots and alert on unexpected changes.
A memory only change is lost at reboot, so a restart may erase the evidence.

objectives: Explain why embedded network devices keep their operating system in a single image.
Describe the difference between changing the stored image and the running memory.
Identify integrity and boot records that reveal an altered system image.
Explain how a modified image can weaken defences or add hidden features.
Compare authorised firmware management with this technique.
Describe the persistence difference between storage and memory modifications.
